title: Letter to Anthropic Re: Planned Initial Public Offering
content:
Letter to Anthropic Re: Planned Initial Public Offering
Dario Amodei
Chief Executive Officer
Anthropic, PBC
500 Howard Street
San Francisco, California
Dear Mr. Amodei:
I write to urge Anthropic to pause its planned initial public offering (IPO) until the company fully and transparently addresses the artificial intelligence (AI) safety, governance, and development pace concerns it has raised. Instead of proceeding headlong with its IPO, the company should focus its energies on addressing these unprecedented risks.
Anthropic and five other companies recently signed a “morally binding” accord with the White House, which is insufficient to meet the moment. Before going public, the company should prioritize addressing the myriad safety concerns surrounding AI threats and establishing a governance regime that matches the seriousness of the concerns being raised by you as well as industry researchers, policymakers, and the public. The demands of preparing for a public offering diverts resources and attention from this very necessary work.
As Comptroller of the City of New York, I serve as investment adviser to, and custodian and a trustee of, the New York City pension funds, which have over $325 billion in assets and constitute one of the largest public pension systems in the United States.
In recent weeks, Anthropic has issued unusually direct public statements acknowledging that the pace of frontier-model capability development may now exceed society’s capacity to understand and control the resulting systems. You have disclosed that unchecked recursive self-improvement could outrun human oversight. In your September 12 essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier,” you stated: “…over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence … We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”
Despite these heightened safety warnings and broad calls for greater caution across the industry, Anthropic reportedly continues to push forward an IPO that could value the company at approximately $2 trillion.
Your essay followed the September 9 resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who publicly said that insiders earnestly believe AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” This claim was supported by Anthropic’s own Alignment Science Lead, Evan Hubinger, who personally thinks the risk is greater than 10% within the next decade.[1]
According to news reports, Anthropic’s draft S‑1 filing warns that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”[2] Reporting also notes that the risk disclosures span 80 pages, nearly twice the length of the section describing the business. These disclosures are not routine and indicate risks that are without precedent, let alone at a public offering of this scale.
Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation with a Long-Term Benefit Trust. Press reports indicate that Anthropic intends to adopt a governance structure that may give founders and trustees concentrated control of the company. A gap between control and accountability is especially concerning for investors given the unprecedented risks the company has already acknowledged.
These concerns underscore the seriousness of the risks at issue. Even if these outcomes prove overstated, such dire warnings illustrate the broad economic risk that imprudent AI advances pose. Addressing the Hugging Face incident specifically, you warned that “in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.”
Considering these concerns, Anthropic should disclose with specificity how it will implement appropriate audits and controls, the scope of what these controls are intended to address, as well as a projected timeline. This should also include an explanation of whether and how these controls will sufficiently address your call to slow the pace at which the capabilities of AI models advance.
In any event, given the gravity of your stated concerns, prudence should not only be shown with respect to the pace of the frontier, it should be also shown with respect to the timing of an IPO.
I therefore urge Anthropic to pause the IPO process so that the company may fully address these key issues, ones which investors must also assess regarding the company’s revised development strategy, governance commitments, and emerging risk landscape.
I request a written response and welcome the opportunity to discuss these matters further.
Sincerely,
Mark D. Levine, New York City Comptroller
[1] https://startupfortune.com/anthropic-researcher-jacob-coxon-quits-warning-ai-could-kill-us-all/; https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ai-kill-humans-anthropic-researcher-more-than-ten-percent-chance/; https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ckgwy1k42w4o
[2] https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/anthropic-warns-ai-may-pose-existential-risks-humanity-ipo-filing-2026-09-29/

report.summary: New York City Comptroller Mark Levine urges Anthropic to pause its reported $2 trillion IPO until it discloses concrete AI safety audits, controls, and governance commitments.
report.background: Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers and maker of the Claude models, has built its public identity around AI safety while raising tens of billions in private capital. It is now reportedly preparing an initial public offering that could value the company at roughly $2 trillion. The letter arrives after a period of unusually blunt warnings from inside Anthropic itself: CEO Dario Amodei's September 12 essay "We Must Pace the Frontier" argued for slowing capability improvements, and researcher Jacob Coxon resigned on September 9 warning that insiders believe AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." Anthropic also signed a voluntary, "morally binding" accord with the White House that critics call unenforceable. Because New York City's pension funds hold over $325 billion in assets, the Comptroller acts as an institutional investor and shareholder advocate, making AI safety a fiduciary question rather than only a policy one.
key_points: Comptroller Mark Levine formally asks Anthropic to halt its IPO until it resolves the safety, governance, and development-pace concerns the company itself has raised. He argues that preparing for a public offering diverts money and management attention away from that safety work, and that prudence about the timing of an IPO should mirror prudence about the pace of the frontier.

The letter leans heavily on Anthropic's own public statements: Amodei's "We Must Pace the Frontier" essay calling for slower capability gains, Jacob Coxon's resignation warning AI could "kill us all by the end of the decade," and Alignment Science Lead Evan Hubinger's stated view that existential risk exceeds 10% within a decade. Levine says these admissions make a $2 trillion listing hard to justify without further explanation.

Anthropic's draft S-1 reportedly contains roughly 80 pages of risk disclosures — nearly twice the length of the section describing the business — including warnings that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." Levine treats this as evidence the offering involves hazards without precedent at this scale, not routine boilerplate.

Governance is a second front. Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation with a Long-Term Benefit Trust, and press reports suggest the planned structure may concentrate control with founders and trustees. Levine warns that a gap between control and accountability is especially dangerous for public investors given the risks the company has already acknowledged.

Levine requests written disclosure of specific audits and controls, their intended scope, and a projected timeline, including whether they would actually slow capability advancement. He also cites Amodei's Hugging Face incident warning that a botnet-capable agent swarm could emerge in 6-12 months and cause hundreds of billions in damage.
report.impact: The letter signals that large institutional investors, especially public pension fiduciaries, now treat frontier AI risk as an investment-risk category rather than a philosophical debate. That raises the disclosure bar for any AI lab seeking public capital: expect longer roadshows, more detailed safety and governance sections in filings, and pressure to name third-party auditors. For developers, it could mean safety evaluations and control timelines becoming gating items attached to financing and enterprise contracts. For regular users, the practical effect is likely slower, more cautious product rollouts and more published documentation about model limits. It also sharpens the tension between voluntary pledges and enforceable obligations, and puts governance structures like benefit corporations and trusts under a public-market microscope.
report.tools: Follow filings and risk factors via SEC EDGAR; read Anthropic's model and system cards plus its Long-Term Benefit Trust documents. For independent evaluation, watch METR's third-party assessments, EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness, and red-teaming tools such as Garak and Meta's Purple Llama. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework offers a governance template, and Anthropic's own interpretability research is worth tracking for how controls might actually be audited.
